title: Write a problem statement and hypothesis
summary: A clear problem statement keeps the team solving the right thing. A hypothesis turns your idea into something you can prove or disprove, so you know later whether it worked.

beginner: Start from your research findings. Pick the user need or pain point with the strongest evidence and the biggest impact.
Write the problem in one or two sentences: who has the problem, what they are trying to do, what stops them, and why it matters. Do not mention a solution yet.
List the evidence under it: research quotes, data, support calls or complaints. If the evidence is thin, say so.
Write a hypothesis in this shape: 'We believe that [doing this] for [these users] will result in [this outcome]. We will know we are right when we see [this measurable signal].'
Pick one or two measures of success you can actually track, and write down the current baseline if you have it.
Note the constraints: policy, legal, technical, budget and deadlines. Then review the statement with your team and change it until everyone agrees.
intermediate: Write a solution-free problem statement grounded in research evidence.
Frame the idea as a testable hypothesis with a clear outcome and signal.
Agree measures of success with baselines, plus known constraints.
Review with design, engineering and stakeholders, and record sign-off.
experienced: Write a problem statement that is solution-free and backed by evidence.
Write a hypothesis that names the users, the change, the outcome and the signal.
Set baselines for success measures, and list constraints and non-goals.
Get sign-off from the team and key stakeholders.

canDelegateTo.task: Draft the problem statement and constraints from the research and process maps
Supply the evidence and check the statement reflects what users said
Find baselines for the measures of success

toolExamples.confluence: Keep the problem statement, hypothesis and measures on one page at the top of your initiative space, and link every later document back to it.
toolExamples.notion: Create a one-page brief with fixed headings: problem, evidence, hypothesis, measures, constraints, non-goals.
toolExamples.google-docs: Share the draft with suggestion mode on, so reviewers propose wording changes rather than overwrite each other.
toolExamples.jira: Paste the hypothesis into the epic description, so it travels with the work into planning.
toolExamples.claude: Paste your research summary and ask for three alternative problem statements that avoid naming a solution. Then ask it to point out where each one lacks evidence.

definitionOfDone: Problem statement agreed and free of any solution
Hypothesis and measures of success agreed, with baselines where possible
pitfalls: Writing the solution into the problem statement
Choosing measures you have no way of tracking
Skipping the baseline, so you cannot tell later whether anything changed
